Please read the research within /papers/investigations-4/10_chern_hopf_integral_estimates and review the manuscript in the precursor project /investigations-3/13_contradiction_analysis/04_boundary_winding/threshold_routes/12_relative_chern_hopf_charges.

I had two new ideas for how to get past some of the obstacles that have arisen in that line of research. Before describing them though, I just want to clarify my understanding. My understanding is that the Chern Hopf integral was not sensitive to a zero of multiplicity 2 vs two separate zeros, which is why it had trouble contributing to the RH implies simple zeros hypothesis. However, it is sensitive to the two zeros being imaginary right? Before they collide?
I’ll read the current investigation and precursor manuscript, then check exactly what the Chern–Hopf integral detects before and at a collision.

The texts distinguish the spatial zero count from the Chern–Hopf collision charge. The spatial count stays two through a double zero; the Chern–Hopf charge is designed to detect the collision. I’m checking how the real-versus-nonreal distinction enters that charge.

**The signed discriminant detects that, yes—but the Chern–Hopf charge itself detects collisions.** Reading the current notes and precursor manuscript also reveals a correction to your first point.

The **ordinary spatial zero count** gives two for both a double zero and two separate simple zeros. The **Chern–Hopf charge of \((H,H_z)\)** distinguishes them: an ordinary double event contributes \(+1\), while a spacetime window containing only simple zeros has charge zero. More generally, a multiplicity-\(m\) heat event contributes \(\binom m2\). See the [manuscript’s charge calculation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-3/13_contradiction_analysis/04_boundary_winding/threshold_routes/12_relative_chern_hopf_charges/manuscript/foundations.tex:149).

For your second point, the relevant signed quantity is
\[
\Delta(t)=(z_1(t)-z_2(t))^2.
\]
For a real-symmetric two-root cluster:

| Configuration | Discriminant |
|---|---:|
| Two distinct real zeros | \(\Delta>0\) |
| A nonreal conjugate pair \(a\pm ib\) | \(\Delta=-4b^2<0\) |
| A double zero | \(\Delta=0\) |

Thus **the sign distinguishes the pair before collision**. “Imaginary” here means an imaginary displacement from their common real center; the zeros need not themselves be purely imaginary.

The exact model makes this transparent:
\[
H(t,z)=(z-a)^2-2t,\qquad \Delta(t)=8t.
\]
For \(t<0\), its roots are \(a\pm i\sqrt{-2t}\); at zero they collide; for \(t>0\), they are two distinct real roots.

However, a collision-free window has Chern–Hopf charge zero on either side. Under the manuscript’s two-root, collar and phase hypotheses, the connection is
\[
Q=\frac{\operatorname{sgn}\Delta(t_+)-\operatorname{sgn}\Delta(t_-)}2.
\]
So the charge registers the **transition**, using those signed endpoint data. See the [real-cap theorem](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-3/13_contradiction_analysis/04_boundary_winding/threshold_routes/12_relative_chern_hopf_charges/manuscript/foundations.tex:282).

The simplicity obstacle is therefore obtaining a theta-specific estimate that **excludes charge one at time zero**. The current integral estimates accommodate that charge. Moreover, RH permits nonreal zeros at negative heat times, so a conjugate pair approaching a hypothetical double at \(t=0\) would be compatible with RH’s reality requirement. See the [current charge evaluation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/10_chern_hopf_integral_estimates/notes/01_ESTABLISHED_MASS_TRACE_AND_AMPLITUDE_RESULTS_20261022.md:79) and the standard [heat-flow threshold framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.05914).
Oh ok, I may have been misinterpreting the difficulty then. So it is possible to detect the double zero, it has just been difficult to rule it out using the known properties of the theta function.
Yes—that’s the distinction. I’ll check the recorded scope once more so I can state what remains missing precisely.

Yes, exactly. **Detecting a hypothetical double zero is understood; excluding it for the actual theta function remains open.**

The local geometry says: *if an ordinary double occurs, its Chern–Hopf charge is one.* The missing step is deriving a restriction from the unchanged theta source that makes that charge impossible at time zero, assuming RH.

The estimates obtained so far remain compatible with the collision. They describe its geometry, mass and singular behavior without producing a contradiction.

One qualification: this concerns **the properties and estimates successfully used so far**. It does not establish that known theta identities are insufficient—there may still be a stronger consequence or combination of them to extract.
What is the analytic form of the sum or integral under investigatin?
I’ll pull out the exact boundary integral and its regularized bulk form, including the theta source they use.

The central **collision-counting integral** is
\[
\boxed{
I_\delta(W)=\frac{2\delta^2}{\pi^2}
\int_W
\frac{\left|H_zH_{zzz}-H_{zz}^{\,2}\right|^2}
{\left(|H|^2+|H_z|^2+\delta^2\right)^3}
\,dA_\tau\,dA_z .
}
\]

Here \(\delta>0\) is a regularization parameter, and \(W\subset\mathbb C_\tau\times\mathbb C_z\) is a bounded window in **complex heat time and complex spectral position**. All derivatives are evaluated at \((\tau,z)\).

The function appearing in it is the canonical theta heat field:
\[
H(\tau,z)=\int_0^\infty e^{\tau u^2}\Phi(u)\cos(zu)\,du,
\]
with
\[
\Phi(u)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty
\left(2\pi^2n^4e^{9u}-3\pi n^2e^{5u}\right)
e^{-\pi n^2e^{4u}},
\qquad H_\tau=-H_{zz}.
\]

Provided \((H,H_z)\ne0\) on the complete boundary of \(W\), its limiting value is
\[
\boxed{
Q_W=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}I_\delta(W)
=\sum_{\substack{p\in W\\H(p)=H_z(p)=0}}
\binom{m_p}{2}.
}
\]
Here \(m_p\) is the spatial multiplicity at the event \(p\). Thus one ordinary double contributes \(1\); simple zeros contribute nothing. These are the [mass and event-sum formulas in the investigation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/notes/04_TOPOLOGICAL_MASS_BOUNDS_AND_INDEX_THEOREM_INTERFACE_20261022.md:23).

The same quantity has the **Chern–Hopf boundary form**
\[
Q_W=\frac1{4\pi^2}\int_{\partial W}\mathcal A\wedge d\mathcal A,
\qquad
\mathcal A=
\frac{\operatorname{Im}\!\left(\overline H\,dH+
                    \overline{H_z}\,dH_z\right)}
{|H|^2+|H_z|^2}.
\]

For a proper finite root cluster in a product window \(W=D\times\Omega\), it also reduces to an ordinary contour integral:
\[
\boxed{
Q_W=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{\partial D}
\frac{\Delta'(\tau)}{\Delta(\tau)}\,d\tau,
\qquad
\Delta(\tau)=\prod_{i<j}\bigl(z_i(\tau)-z_j(\tau)\bigr)^2.
}
\]
This is the [manuscript’s discriminant-winding identity](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-3/13_contradiction_analysis/04_boundary_winding/threshold_routes/12_relative_chern_hopf_charges/manuscript/foundations.tex:63).

These are three representations of the same charge: **a nonnegative bulk integral in the regularization limit, a boundary integral, and a sum of collision multiplicities.**
In the last formula, what are z_i labeling?
The indices enumerate the zeros in the selected finite cluster, counting multiplicity.

For each fixed heat time \(\tau\), the quantities
\[
z_1(\tau),\ldots,z_m(\tau)
\]
are the **zeros of \(H(\tau,z)\) inside the chosen spatial region \(\Omega\)**, counted with multiplicity:
\[
H(\tau,z_i(\tau))=0.
\]

The indices simply enumerate those roots. The product
\[
\Delta(\tau)=\prod_{i<j}(z_i(\tau)-z_j(\tau))^2
\]
includes each unordered pair once.

For a two-root cluster:

- Two distinct simple zeros have \(z_1\ne z_2\), hence \(\Delta\ne0\).
- At a double zero, \(z_1=z_2\), hence \(\Delta=0\).

Individual labels can exchange when \(\tau\) travels around a collision. The discriminant is unchanged by relabeling, so it remains a well-defined holomorphic function of \(\tau\).
And the spatial region \Omega is a region in the complex plane? And presumably for this definition of H assuming RH the zeros are on the real line?
Yes—\(\Omega\) lies in the complex \(z\)-plane. RH gives real zeros at heat time zero, and the heat-flow theorem extends that reality to positive real times.

Yes. **\(\Omega\) is a region in the complex \(z\)-plane**, typically a disk
\[
\Omega=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-a|<R\},
\]
with \(a\) real when studying a possible collision on the real axis.

And **RH says precisely that all zeros of \(H(0,z)\) are real**, because
\[
H(0,z)=\frac18\,\xi\!\left(\frac12+\frac{iz}{2}\right).
\]
A zeta zero \(\rho=\frac12+i\gamma\) therefore corresponds to the real zero \(z=2\gamma\).

The qualification concerns heat time:

- At \(\tau=0\): RH gives real zeros; their simplicity remains open.
- For real \(\tau>0\): under RH, the zeros are real and simple.
- For negative real or nonreal complex \(\tau\): that reality conclusion does not apply.

These distinctions are stated in the [manuscript’s normalization and RH discussion](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-3/13_contradiction_analysis/04_boundary_winding/threshold_routes/12_relative_chern_hopf_charges/manuscript/introduction.tex:67).

So \(\Omega\) remains a two-dimensional complex region even when the zeros it encloses happen to lie on its real diameter.
But if A is a one form, then A\wedge dA is a three form, but it is integrated on the boundary of a three dimensional space, hence 2-d, unless time is complex here?
Yes—time is complex in that formula. The domain has four real dimensions, so its boundary has three.

**Yes—time is complex in this Chern–Hopf construction.** Write
\[
\tau=t+is,\qquad z=x+iy.
\]
Then
\[
W=D\times\Omega\subset\mathbb C_\tau\times\mathbb C_z
\cong\mathbb R^4,
\]
so \(\partial W\) has **three real dimensions**, matching the three-form \(\mathcal A\wedge d\mathcal A\).

Its boundary consists of
\[
\partial W=(\partial D\times\Omega)\cup(D\times\partial\Omega),
\]
whose pieces have dimensions \(1+2=3\) and \(2+1=3\).

Your dimensional objection would be correct **if time were restricted to a real interval**: \([t_-,t_+]\times\Omega\) would have dimension three, its boundary dimension two, and the displayed three-form boundary integral would not apply.

The physical heat evolution uses real time. The charge construction uses its holomorphic extension to complex time; the real-time statements and cap signs are then extracted from that larger setting.

So I was reading that the Pair Correlation Conjecture implies the simple zeros hypothesis. What if your region went to infty and you could prove that PCC holds at infty, so that the integral is 0 at infty, but then since the sides vanish then maybe you could use that to argue that you can't have a non-zero winding at t=0?
I’ll check exactly what pair correlation implies about multiplicities, then examine whether an expanding Chern–Hopf boundary could turn that information into zero charge at time zero.

The first distinction matters: standard PCC implies that asymptotically 100% of zeros are simple, which still allows isolated or sparse multiple zeros. I’m checking whether the unnormalized topological charge supplies the extra information your argument needs.
I'm not assuming PCC at zero, I'm thinking maybe you could prove that asymptotically PCC holds, which could help you constrain the cap integral

Understood—you mean proving an asymptotic correlation law and using it to estimate the distant cap, then transferring that estimate toward time zero. I’ll focus on that proposed link between pair statistics and cap flux.

Which limit do you have in mind for the asymptotic pair correlation: large real heat time t → +∞, or large zero height |Re z| → ∞ with heat time fixed?
- Large real heat time
- Large zero height

Then the relevant question is whether large-heat-time zero statistics control the complex-time cap. The existing research has late-time asymptotics for fixed groups of zeros; I’m checking what they say about that cap.

For fixed groups of zeros, the recorded large-heat-time limit is equally spaced and cosine-like. It remains compatible with a double at time zero. I’m using the write-page skill to save the assessment in the investigation’s notes, focusing on what additional estimate would turn those late-time data into a bound on the complete cap.

**Yes—a theorem about large real heat time could help constrain the distant cap.** I initially focused on standard PCC, whose asymptotic parameter is zero height. Your proposal asks for a different asymptotic theorem for \(H(T,\cdot)\) as \(T\to+\infty\). [Montgomery’s formulation](https://websites.umich.edu/~hlm/paircor1.pdf).

The crucial step would be connecting those zero statistics to the actual cap integral
\[
I_T=\int_{\{\,\operatorname{Re}\tau=T\,\}\times[-Y,Y]_{\operatorname{Im}\tau}\times\Omega}
\mathcal C.
\]
That cap also sees **imaginary-time phase**, which real-root spacing statistics do not directly describe.

A useful exact check is
\[
H(\tau,z)=e^\tau\cos z.
\]
Its zeros are always simple and equally spaced. Nevertheless, writing \(\tau=t+is\), \(z=x+iy\), its three-form is
\[
\mathcal C=
\frac{\operatorname{sech}^2(2y)}{2\pi^2}\,
ds\wedge dx\wedge dy.
\]
On a rectangular cap with \(|s|\le Y\), \(|x|\le X\), \(|y|\le B\),
\[
I_T=\frac{2XY\tanh(2B)}{\pi^2},
\]
independent of \(T\), although the connecting-side integrals vanish. The factor \(e^\tau\) retains the phase \(e^{is}\) after normalization.

This model does **not** rule out a theta-specific estimate. It shows why even very regular late-time zero statistics need not make the raw cap integral zero. They might instead determine a nonzero reference value and bound its remainder.

There is also an event term in the transport identity:
\[
I_T-I_{-\varepsilon}+I_{\rm sides}
=
Q_W
=
\sum_{p\in W}\binom{m_p}{2}.
\]
Consequently, vanishing late-cap and side integrals alone would leave the early-cap contribution. That contribution—or a small linking boundary around the candidate collision—must also be retained.

So the useful version of your idea is: **derive a sufficiently precise late-time cap estimate, combine it with controlled connecting and initial terms, and bound the complete charge.** A complete absolute bound below \(1\) would force its nonnegative integer value to be zero. The missing theorem is that quantitative passage from late-time statistics to complete flux; the proposal does not require assuming PCC at time zero.

I saved the calculations and scope in this [research note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/10_chern_hopf_integral_estimates/notes/03_LATE_HEAT_PAIR_STATISTICS_AND_CAP_FLUX_20261022.md).
How would you bound the complete charge if you could bound the cap with asymptotic PCC and prove the sides vanish (which I think they do if the sides follow zeros)?
I’ll separate the charge identity from the assumptions needed for the cap and sides, and check what changes when the sides move with the zeros.

If the cap were the only nonzero contribution to a regular enclosing boundary, an upper bound below \(1\) would force zero charge. A tube joining early and late times also has an early cap to account for. The notes do give exact constructions with vanishing sides, but they retain that cap or a linking boundary around the collision.

**If the cap and the vanishing sides constitute the entire regular boundary enclosing the candidate collision, the argument is direct:**
\[
Q=\int_{\partial W}\mathcal C
  =I_{\rm cap}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.
\]
A proved upper bound
\[
I_{\rm cap}<1
\]
would force \(Q=0\), excluding the collision. An asymptotic limit of zero would be more than enough.

For a tube joining early and late heat times, however, there are **two caps**:
\[
Q=I_T-I_-+I_{\rm sides}.
\]
Thus estimates
\[
I_T\le U_T,\qquad I_-\ge L_-,\qquad
|I_{\rm sides}|\le\varepsilon_T
\]
give
\[
\boxed{0\le Q\le U_T-L_-+\varepsilon_T.}
\]
Making the right side strictly less than \(1\) proves zero charge. This also allows a nonzero asymptotic baseline: if both caps are close enough to the same known value, their difference can still give the required bound.

Your intuition about sides following zeros has a precise realization. In the chart \(H_z\ne0\), a regular side defined by
\[
\left|\frac{H}{H_z}\right|=\epsilon
\]
has **exactly zero Chern–Hopf flux**. Its projective image lies in a circle, so the pulled-back curvature vanishes. These surfaces can form tubes around simple zero branches. An arbitrary moving contour around the zeros does not automatically satisfy that condition. See the [projective-side lemma](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/notes/01_CHERN_HOPF_PROJECTIVE_SIDES_AND_LOCAL_SECTORS_20261022.md:45).

The delicate point is where the zeros collide: both \(H\) and \(H_z\) vanish, so that ratio chart fails. The tube must be closed using another chart or a small linking boundary; its contribution cannot simply be discarded as its size shrinks.

A clean formulation of your proposed proof would therefore be:

1. Assume an ordinary double at time zero. Its small linking three-sphere has charge \(1\).
2. Transfer that boundary to a distant cap, retaining every connecting piece and losing no event through the boundary.
3. Prove the connectors vanish and the distant cap has integral \(<1\).

Then Stokes would give
\[
1=I_{\rm distant\ cap}<1,
\]
a contradiction. **That is a valid conditional strategy.** The substantive tasks are establishing the complete tube geometry and deriving the cap estimate from the late-time theta statistics.
